Clifford Geertz. The American anthropologist who pioneered interpretive anthropology, arguing that cultural analysis is fundamentally a hermeneutic practice — reading culture as a text to uncover meaning rather than identifying universal laws.

Geertz introduced thick description, the idea that ethnographic writing must capture not just behavior but the layers of meaning, context, and intention surrounding it. He developed interpretive anthropology, also called symbolic or hermeneutic anthropology, explicitly rejecting positivist models of science in favor of meaning-centered analysis.

He conducted extended fieldwork in Indonesia and Morocco. In Bali, he analyzed cockfighting as a window into Balinese concepts of self and status. That single cultural practice, seemingly narrow, opened into an entire interpretation of how Balinese people understand identity and social rank.

Geertz approached religion not as a system of beliefs to be catalogued, but as cultural meaning-making. This influenced how anthropologists approach ritual and cosmology across all traditions. He wrote for wide academic and public audiences; his essays on nationalism, art, and modernity became central to cultural studies and literary theory, reaching far beyond the discipline of anthropology itself.

He insisted on the observer effect in ethnography — that the anthropologist's presence, subjective positioning, and interpretive choices shape ethnographic knowledge. This was a crucial acknowledgment that ethnography is not objective documentation but collaborative interpretation.
